title: The Robot Soccer Team
summary: A school robotics team must find and fix a bug in their robot's code the night before a robot-soccer match.
poll: Finding a small mistake is often harder than building the whole project.

versions.title: The Robot Soccer Team
versions.text:
Sara and Omar are in the robot club. They built a small robot. Its name is Spark.

Spark can play soccer. Tomorrow is a big robot match. It is called the City Cup.

Tonight, the team tests Spark one more time. Spark must run to the ball. Then it must kick the ball. But Spark does not kick it. Spark spins and spins! It will not stop.

Omar looks at the code. Code tells a robot what to do. Omar reads the code line by line. He finds a bug! The code tells Spark to turn. But it never tells Spark to stop turning.

Omar fixes the bug. He adds one small line. Now the code tells Spark when to stop.

They test Spark again. Spark turns once. Then it runs to the ball. Spark kicks the ball! It goes into the goal.

Sara and Omar cheer. The team claps too. Spark is ready for the big match.

versions.title: The Robot Soccer Team
versions.text:
Sara and Omar are in the robotics club at their school. Together they built a small robot named Spark. Spark was built to play in a robot-soccer match.

Tomorrow is the big match. It is called the City Robotics Cup. The whole team wants Spark to do well against the other schools.

Tonight, the night before the match, the team tests Spark one last time. Spark is supposed to run toward the ball. Then it should kick the ball into the goal. Instead, Spark just spins around and around in one spot. No matter what the team tries, Spark will not stop turning.

Worried, Omar opens his laptop and looks at Spark's code. Code is a set of exact steps. It tells a robot what to do, one step after another. Omar reads through each line slowly, looking for a mistake. At last, he finds the bug. The code tells Spark to turn. But it never tells Spark when that turning should stop.

Omar fixes the bug. He types one small line that had been missing. Now the code clearly tells Spark exactly when to stop turning.

The team tests Spark once more. This time, Spark turns only once. Then it runs straight toward the ball and kicks it hard. The ball sails right into the goal!

Sara and Omar cheer with relief. The rest of the team claps and laughs. Spark is ready for tomorrow's important match.

versions.title: The Robot Soccer Team
versions.text:
Sara and Omar lead their school's robotics club. Together they spent weeks building a small robot named Spark. Spark was built for a robot-soccer competition.

Tomorrow is the big match. It is called the Robotics Cup, and teams from across the city will take part. The whole team is counting on Spark to do well.

Tonight, the night before the match, the team gathers to test Spark one last time. Spark is supposed to run toward the ball and kick it cleanly into the goal. Instead, Spark just spins around and around in one spot. No matter how many times the team restarts it, Spark will not stop turning.

Worried, Omar opens his laptop and studies Spark's code line by line. Code is a set of exact steps. It tells a robot precisely what to do, one step after another, with no room for guessing. Spark's sensor can see the ball just fine, and its motor spins the wheels just fine too, so Omar knows he must debug the program itself. After several minutes of careful reading, Omar finds the bug. The code tells Spark to turn. But it never tells Spark when that turning should stop. So Spark just keeps turning, again and again, forever.

Omar quickly fixes the bug. He types one small line that had been missing from the program. Now the code clearly tells Spark exactly when to stop turning and move forward toward the ball.

The team tests Spark once more, holding their breath. This time, Spark turns only once. Then it runs straight toward the ball and kicks it hard. The ball sails past the goalkeeper and into the goal!

Sara and Omar cheer with relief. The rest of the team claps and laughs, glad that Spark is finally ready for tomorrow's important match.

versions.title: The Robot Soccer Team
versions.text:
Sara and Omar lead their school's robotics club. Together, they spent several weeks building a small robot named Spark for a robot-soccer competition.

Tomorrow afternoon is the big match. It is called the Robotics Cup, and teams from schools across the city will take part. The whole team is counting on Spark to do well.

Tonight, the night before the match, the team gathers to test Spark one last time. Spark is supposed to roll toward the ball and kick it cleanly into the goal. Instead, to everyone's surprise, Spark just spins around and around in one spot. No matter how many times the team restarts the robot, Spark will not stop turning.

Worried, Omar opens his laptop and studies Spark's code line by line, looking for whatever has gone wrong. Code is a set of exact steps. It tells a robot precisely what to do, one step after another, with no room for guessing. Spark's sensor can see the ball just fine, and its motor spins the wheels just fine too, so neither of those parts is the problem. Omar realizes he must debug the program itself. After several minutes of careful, frustrating reading, Omar finds the bug. The code correctly tells Spark to turn. But it never tells Spark when that turning should stop. So the robot just keeps turning, again and again, trapped in what some people call an endless loop.

Omar quickly fixes the bug. He types one small line that had been missing from the program. Now the code clearly tells Spark exactly when to stop turning and move forward toward the ball instead.

The team tests Spark once more, holding their breath as the robot powers on. This time, Spark turns only once. Then it rolls straight toward the ball and kicks it with real force. The ball sails past the goalkeeper and lands inside the goal!

Sara and Omar cheer with relief. The rest of the team claps and laughs, glad that Spark is finally ready for tomorrow's important match.

No matter how many times the team restarts the robot, it refuses to stop turning, almost as if something invisible is controlling it.

It tells a robot precisely what to do, one step after another, leaving no room for guessing. Spark's sensor can see the ball just fine, and its motor spins the wheels just fine too, so Omar knows he must debug the program itself, not the robot's parts. After several minutes of careful, frustrating reading, Omar finds the bug. The code correctly tells Spark to turn. But it never tells Spark when that turning should stop. So the robot keeps repeating the same turn, trapped in what programmers call an endless loop.

Omar quickly fixes the bug. He types one small, missing line into the program. Now the code clearly tells Spark exactly when to stop turning and move forward toward the ball instead.

The team tests Spark once more, holding their breath as the small robot powers on. This time, Spark turns only once. Then it rolls straight toward the ball and kicks it with real force. The ball sails past the goalkeeper and lands inside the goal!

Sara and Omar cheer with relief. The rest of the team claps and laughs, finally confident that Spark is ready for tomorrow's important match against the other schools.

versions.title: The Robot Soccer Team
versions.text:
Sara and Omar are the two student leaders of their school's robotics club, and together they had spent several weeks designing, building, and carefully programming a small robot named Spark for a robot-soccer competition.

Tomorrow afternoon is the big match, known across the region as the Robotics Cup, and teams from rival schools will take part. The whole team is counting on Spark to perform well.

Tonight, the night before the match, the team gathers to test Spark one last time, before the deadline arrives. Spark is supposed to roll steadily toward the ball and kick it cleanly into the goal, just as it had practiced many times before. Instead, to everyone's growing alarm, Spark just spins around and around in one spot. No matter how many times the team restarts the robot, it refuses to stop turning, almost as if something invisible has taken control of it.

Worried, Omar opens his laptop and studies Spark's code line by line, patiently looking for whatever has gone wrong inside the program. Code is a set of exact steps that tells a robot precisely what to do, one step after another, leaving no room for guessing or assuming. Spark's sensor can see the ball just fine, and its motor spins the wheels just fine too, so Omar knows the problem must be hidden in the program, which means he has to debug it carefully. After several minutes of careful, frustrating reading, Omar finally finds the bug: the code correctly tells Spark to turn, but it never tells Spark when that turning should stop, so the robot keeps repeating the same turn, trapped in what programmers call an endless loop.

Omar quickly fixes the bug by typing one small, missing line into the program, an instruction the earlier version had somehow left out. Now the code clearly tells Spark exactly when to stop turning and move forward toward the ball instead.

The team tests Spark once more, holding their breath as the small robot powers on. This time, Spark turns only once. Then it rolls straight toward the ball and kicks it with real, satisfying force. The ball sails past the goalkeeper and lands inside the goal!

Sara and Omar cheer with relief. The rest of the team claps and laughs, finally confident that Spark is ready for tomorrow's important match against the other schools.

versions.title: The Robot Soccer Team
versions.text:
Sara and Omar, the two student leaders of their school's robotics club, had spent several weeks designing, building, and carefully programming a small robot named Spark for a robot-soccer competition. They poured far more hours into the project than anyone outside the club realized.

Tomorrow afternoon brings the big match, known across the region as the Robotics Cup. Teams from rival schools will take part, and the whole team is counting on Spark to perform well against them.

Tonight, the night before the match, the team gathers one final time to test Spark, before the deadline arrives. According to the plan, Spark should roll steadily toward the ball and kick it cleanly into the goal, exactly as it had practiced many times before. Instead, to everyone's growing alarm, Spark simply spins around and around in one spot, refusing to advance at all. No matter how many times the team restarts the robot, it stubbornly keeps turning, almost as though some invisible force has taken control of its movements.

Worried, Omar opens his laptop and studies Spark's algorithm line by line, patiently searching for whatever has gone wrong. An algorithm is a sequence of exact instructions. It tells a robot precisely what to do, one step after another, leaving no room for guessing or assuming. A good engineer has to calibrate every sensor and check each variable the program uses, especially in an autonomous robot like Spark that has to act on its own during the match, with no one controlling it directly. After several minutes of careful, frustrating reading, Omar finally locates the bug. The code correctly instructs Spark to turn, but it never specifies when that turning should stop. So the robot keeps repeating the identical turn, trapped in what programmers call an endless loop.

Omar swiftly corrects the bug by typing one small, missing line into the program, an instruction the earlier version had somehow left out. Now the code clearly specifies exactly when Spark should stop turning and begin moving forward toward the ball instead.

The team tests Spark once more, holding their breath as the small robot powers on. This time, Spark turns only once, rolls straight toward the ball, and kicks it with real, satisfying force. The ball sails past the goalkeeper and lands inside the goal.

Sara and Omar cheer with relief, and the rest of the team claps and laughs, finally confident that Spark is ready for tomorrow's important match against its rivals.

versions.title: The Robot Soccer Team
versions.text:
Sara and Omar, the two student leaders of their school's robotics club, had devoted several weeks to designing, constructing, and meticulously programming a small robot named Spark for an upcoming robot-soccer competition, investing far more hours into the project than anyone outside the club ever fully appreciated.

Tomorrow afternoon brings the decisive match, known throughout the city as the Robotics Cup, and the entire team is depending on Spark to perform admirably against robots engineered by rival schools from across the region, each team fervently hoping its machine will ultimately outperform the rest.

Tonight, the evening before the match, the team convenes one final time to test Spark thoroughly before the approaching deadline. According to their meticulously rehearsed plan, Spark should roll steadily toward the ball and kick it cleanly into the goal, exactly as it had practiced countless times previously. Instead, to everyone's mounting alarm, Spark simply spins around and around in one spot, refusing to advance whatsoever! No matter how many times the team restarts the robot, it stubbornly continues turning, almost as though some invisible force has seized complete control of its movements.

Genuinely alarmed, Omar opens his laptop and studies Spark's algorithm line by line, searching patiently for whatever has malfunctioned inside the program. An algorithm is simply a sequence of exact instructions that directs a robot precisely what to do, one step after another, leaving absolutely no room for guessing or assuming anything whatsoever. A competent engineer must calibrate every sensor and verify each variable the program relies upon, especially in an autonomous robot that has to act entirely on its own during the match, without anyone controlling it directly. After several minutes of careful, increasingly frustrating examination, Omar finally locates the culprit: the code correctly instructs Spark to turn, yet it never specifies a condition for when that turning should cease, so the robot simply keeps repeating the identical turn indefinitely, trapped in what programmers call an endless loop.

Omar swiftly corrects the bug by typing one small, missing line into the program, a single instruction the earlier version had somehow omitted entirely. Now the code clearly specifies the precise moment Spark should cease turning and begin moving forward toward the ball instead.

The team tests Spark once more, holding their breath nervously as the small robot powers on. This time, Spark turns only once, rolls straight toward the ball, and kicks it with surprising, satisfying force. The ball sails cleanly past the goalkeeper and lands inside the goal!

Sara and Omar cheer with relief, and the rest of the team claps and laughs with delight, finally confident that Spark is thoroughly prepared for tomorrow's decisive match against its rivals.

keyWords.definition: a machine that can be told what to do and can move or work on its own
keyWords.example: The robot moved across the floor to pick up the box.

keyWords.definition: a list of steps that tells a computer or robot what to do
keyWords.example: She wrote code to make the toy car turn left.

keyWords.definition: a group of people who work together on the same goal
keyWords.example: Our team practiced every day before the game.

keyWords.definition: to hit something with your foot
keyWords.example: He kicked the ball across the yard.

keyWords.definition: to repair something or make it work correctly
keyWords.example: Dad had to fix the broken chair.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A team that builds a brand new school building
A team that fixes a robot's code before a match
A team that paints a large wall mural downtown
A team that plants a new flower garden
questions.why: The story is about Sara and Omar fixing a bug in Spark's code before the robot soccer match.

wrong.A: The story is not about building a school.
wrong.C: The story does not mention painting.
wrong.D: The story does not mention planting.

questions.stem: What does Spark do instead of kicking the ball?
options: It stops moving suddenly
It runs away quickly
It spins in circles
It falls over sideways
questions.why: The story says Spark spins around and around instead of kicking the ball.

wrong.A: Spark keeps moving, it does not stop.
wrong.B: Spark does not run away in the story.
wrong.D: The story does not say Spark falls over.

questions.stem: Why does Spark keep spinning?
options: The team turned it off completely
The battery is too weak to work
The ball is too far away to reach
The code never tells it to stop
questions.why: Omar finds that the code tells Spark to turn but never tells it to stop.

wrong.A: The team does not turn Spark off.
wrong.B: The story does not say the battery is weak.
wrong.C: The distance to the ball is not the problem.

questions.stem: Who finds the bug in the code?
options: Omar
Sara
The coach
A judge
questions.why: The story says Omar studies the code and finds the bug.

wrong.B: Sara watches, but Omar reads the code.
wrong.C: No coach is named in the story.
wrong.D: No judge is named in the story.

questions.stem: What does Omar do to fix the bug?
options: He buys a brand-new robot instead of the old one
He adds a small missing line to the code
He paints Spark a new color design on its back
He asks another team for some help with the code
questions.why: Omar types one small, missing line into the program to fix the bug.

wrong.A: The team keeps the same robot, Spark.
wrong.C: The story does not mention paint.
wrong.D: The story does not mention asking another team.

questions.stem: What happens after Omar fixes the code?
options: The team gives up and goes home sad
Spark stops working completely for good, today
Spark starts spinning even faster now, and nonstop
Spark turns once, then runs and kicks the ball in
questions.why: After the fix, Spark turns once, runs to the ball, and kicks it into the goal.

wrong.A: The team cheers instead of giving up.
wrong.B: Spark works well after the fix.
wrong.C: Spark does not spin faster; it stops spinning.

questions.stem: How do Sara and Omar most likely feel when the ball goes into the goal?
options: Angry and confused
Happy and relieved
Bored and tired
Scared and worried
questions.why: The story says they cheer, which shows they feel happy and relieved.

wrong.A: The story does not describe anger at that moment.
wrong.C: They are not described as bored.
wrong.D: Their worry ends once the fix works.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about the night before the match?
options: To describe what the team eats for dinner before the game
To show how the team solves a problem under pressure
To explain the official rules of soccer to new readers
To describe the weather outside that night and the dark sky
questions.why: The story focuses on the team finding and fixing the bug just before the deadline.

wrong.A: The story does not describe dinner.
wrong.C: The story does not explain soccer rules.
wrong.D: The story does not describe the weather.

LOW.prompt: Have you ever had to fix a mistake before an important event? Write about it, or imagine how you would feel if you were Omar fixing the code.
checklist: I clearly described a mistake and a fix.
I used at least two details from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: If I were Omar, I would feel worried when Spark kept spinning in circles. I would read the code carefully, just like he did, to find the bug. When I found the missing line and fixed it, I would feel proud and relieved, because the team worked hard to be ready for the match.

MID.prompt: Explain the problem the robotics team faced and how Omar solved it. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how it was solved, using at least two details.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The robotics team faced a serious problem the night before their competition: their robot, Spark, would not stop spinning in one spot instead of kicking the ball. Omar studied the program's code line by line and discovered that the turning instruction had no stop condition, so it kept repeating forever. He solved the problem by typing in the one small, missing line the program needed, which told Spark exactly when to stop turning and move toward the ball.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says finding a small mistake is often harder than building the whole project. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Spark's bug.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that finding a small mistake can be harder than building the whole project in the first place. In the story, Sara and Omar had already spent weeks designing and building Spark, yet one missing line in the algorithm, impossible to see from the outside, caused the robot to spin endlessly. Omar had to read through the entire program line by line just to locate that single flaw. Someone might argue that building the robot required far more total effort than fixing one line, and that is true, but the search for the bug demanded a different kind of difficulty: patient, careful attention to detail that building alone did not require.
